item.content:encoded:
By Maureen Nzai and Peter Kigwilu

On October 26, the university community gathered in the Auditorium for a Town Hall Meeting on the Self-Assessment Report prepared for the Commission for University Education’s (CUE’s) Institutional Quality Audit of the university.

Prof. Jeremiah Koshal, Ag. Deputy Vice Chancellor, Academics – Transformative Teaching, Learning and Research, the moderator of the meeting, opened the session by welcoming the Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Mwenda Ntarangwi, who commended the self-study Team for preparing a comprehensive report, which he likened in several ways to that submitted to WSCUC for accreditation re-affirmation scheduled for 11-13 November, 2026. Thereafter, Prof. Peter Kigwilu, Director of Quality Assurance, presented the report’s highlights, and the session closed with a question-and-answer segment moderated by Prof. Koshal.

The presentation outlined a 13-month, evidence-based self-study covering ten chapters and fourteen quality aspects. The report noted that since the institutional quality audit in 2021, academic programs have grown from 31 to 49, enrolment has risen to 8,263 students, and annual publications have increased from 137 to 197. Further, the university has posted a surplus every year, and about 80% of full-time faculty hold doctorates. The university remains the only one in Eastern and Central Africa with dual accreditation.

The report acknowledged challenges that the university is focused on addressing: declining employment among recent undergraduate graduates, reliance on tuition for about 69% of income, over-reliance on adjunct faculty, limited hostel capacity, and accessibility gaps in older buildings. Each is matched by a response in the five-year Quality Plan, whose 30 actions include raising full-time faculty teaching from 52% to 65% of courses and undergraduate employment to at least 70% by 2030/31.

The report will be submitted to CUE on October 30, ahead of the audit visit on December 7-11, 2026. Colleagues were thanked for their contributions and encouraged to read and give feedback necessary to enhance the report.

item.content:encoded:
By Njoki Chege

USIU-Africa recently marked Deaf Awareness Day 2026, bringing together students, faculty, staff, university leaders, partners, volunteers, and members of the Deaf community under the theme, Declaring Deaf People’s Human Rights. The collaborative event between the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at USIU-Africa and Equity Group Foundation provided a platform to discuss Deaf people’s human rights, accessibility, communication, and participation. The event featured Kenyan Sign Language presentations, songs, poems, a panel discussion, and a skit by learners from St. Luke’s Primary School for the Deaf, Embu.

Speaking during the event, Zablon Kengara of Light for the World emphasized the need to involve Deaf people in developing solutions that affect their lives. He also commended USIU-Africa for its inclusive approach towards students with disabilities, sharing his personal experience of having to pay for a sign language interpreter during his studies, which made it difficult.

The panel discussion brought together Washington Akaranga, a KSL researcher and sign language training coordinator at the University of Nairobi; Jerioth Wanjiku of Equity Group Foundation; Winnie Kihanya, a USIU-Africa alumnus and disability inclusion advocate; and Dr. Jefwa Mweri of the Kenyan Sign Language Research Project at the University of Nairobi.  Raziyah Mwihaki, a student pursuing Applied Computer Technology, moderated the session, where the focus was on exploring how technology, education and curriculum design, financial services and communities can be made more inclusive. Akaranga noted that Kenya has made significant progress in advancing the rights and inclusion of Deaf people, while emphasizing the need to build on these gains by ensuring Deaf people are actively involved in designing systems and solutions that affect them.

The event also featured a community service initiative, through which four whiteboards and five shaving machines were donated to St. Luke’s Primary School for the Deaf. The school was represented by 30 students, six teachers, and the Head Teacher, Michael Nyaga.

The session underscored USIU-Africa’s commitment to fostering an inclusive university community while highlighting the importance of partnerships in advancing meaningful participation and opportunities for persons with disabilities.

Facilitated by Sandra Akello and David Okinyi from the Arizona...
item.content:encoded:
By Njoki Chege

The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at USIU-Africa hosted a Baobab Roadshow on October 15, bringing together current scholars, finalists, and alumni to explore opportunities available through the Baobab Platform and learn how to leverage its resources for their personal and professional development. Facilitated by Sandra Akello and David Okinyi from the Arizona State University Baobab team, the roadshow provided a platform for participants to learn more about the opportunities available within the Baobab community, including career development resources, professional networking, and continued engagement beyond university.

Two separate sessions were conducted to address the different needs of participants at various levels of their academic and professional journeys. The first session targeted current Mastercard Foundation Scholars and introduced them to the platform’s features, resources, and opportunities. Participants explored how the platform could help them build connections, access relevant opportunities, and prepare for their transition into the professional world. The second session brought together senior students in their final year of study and alumni. It focused on the value of remaining connected to the Baobab community beyond the completion of university studies and encouraged participants to explore how the platform could support their continued professional growth, networking, and engagement with opportunities.

To reinforce learning and encourage active participation, the sessions incorporated an interactive Kahoot quiz that tested participants’ understanding of the Baobab Platform. The activity introduced an element of friendly competition while helping participants reflect on the information shared during the sessions. The roadshow concluded with an award ceremony recognizing the top performers in the quiz. The roadshow was supported by the USIU-Africa Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program team and Baobab Ambassadors Yeebyo Legese, Lydia Arime, Kwalya Morgan, Jean Daniel Kwizera, and Jacob Yen Alier. Their involvement helped facilitate engagement and strengthen connections among participants and the wider Baobab community.

Through initiatives such as the Baobab Roadshow, the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program continues to create opportunities for Scholars to access networks, resources, and platforms that support their growth during and beyond their university education.

item.title: USIU-Africa Alumnus and Prof. Paul Okanda publish a study on keeping track of changing market rules
item.dc:creator: akaka
item.description: By CTW Team Oliver Njeru, a USIU-Africa alumnus who earned a Bachelor of Science in Applied Computer Technology in 2025, has published a peer-reviewed research paper with Prof. Paul Okanda, Associate Professor of Information Systems and Technology at the School of Science and Technology. The paper, Market data governance as knowledge management: managing temporality via...
item.content:encoded:
By CTW Team

Oliver Njeru, a USIU-Africa alumnus who earned a Bachelor of Science in Applied Computer Technology in 2025, has published a peer-reviewed research paper with Prof. Paul Okanda, Associate Professor of Information Systems and Technology at the School of Science and Technology. The paper, Market data governance as knowledge management: managing temporality via rule versioning, provenance and auditability, was accepted on September 9, 2026, and made available online on October 20, 2026, in the VINE Journal of Information and Knowledge Management Systems, an international journal published by Emerald.

Financial markets run on rules that change. Trading fees are revised, holiday calendars shift, and data suppliers alter their formats. If a computer system cannot tell which rule applied on a given day, its analysis of the past can be wrong without anyone noticing, and the error often surfaces only after the results have been used.

The study examined a research codebase for stock trading that the authors built for an earlier project and ran on synthetic data. It shows how such rules can be stored in software together with the dates they apply, so that past results can be replayed and checked. From this case, the authors propose five design practices for teams that handle market data, such as keeping each rule with its dates and writing down what a system does not do. Their code and evidence are public, so anyone can check the paper’s claims.

The paper suggests that these practices can give organizations without specialized data tools, including many in emerging markets, basic traceability using an ordinary code repository.

The road to publication was demanding. Between February and September 2026, the paper went through four editorial decisions. In one round, a reviewer recommended rejection, but the editor asked for another revision instead. Each round pushed the authors to narrow their claims and support every statement with evidence. Njeru wrote the software and led the analysis and writing while Prof. Okanda supervised and reviewed the work.

Today, Njeru is an independent researcher, the founder of Black Eternum Capital, and a founding engineer at Replicant Trader. “I believe I have kept my word to work on and provide a high-quality research paper to be published in a journal, and earned my place in the research field,” Njeru said. “This means a lot to me.”

Prof. Okanda congratulated Njeru on having earned [his] rightful place in academic research, noting that the paper took the better part of a year and grit, patience and focus to publish. “I hope this is just the beginning,” he noted. Advising students who are hoping to publish, he stated, “Choose one clear question and make your evidence easy to check. Treat tough reviews as free help, not a final verdict. Submit early. Do HARD things!”

To read the full article, visit: https://doi.org/10.1108/VJIKMS-03-2026-0132 OR https://olivernjeru.github.io/publications.html

Publication: Njeru, O., & Okanda, P. (2026). Market data governance as knowledge management: Managing temporality via rule versioning, provenance and auditability. VINE Journal of Information and Knowledge Management Systems. https://doi.org/10.1108/VJIKMS-03-2026-0132

item.title: USIU-Africa faculty member publishes research on health sciences curriculum innovation

The article examines the opportunities, challenges, and lessons learned from developing innovative health sciences academic programs. The publication, titled Reflective Analysis of...
item.content:encoded:
By CTW Team

Dr. Ermias Mergia Terefe, Assistant Professor of Pharmacology and Therapeutics at United States International University-Africa, has published a research article in Discover Education, a peer-reviewed journal published by Springer Nature. The article examines the opportunities, challenges, and lessons learned from developing innovative health sciences academic programs.

The publication, titled Reflective Analysis of Health Sciences Curriculum Innovation at a Kenyan University, draws on his experience in the collaborative development of three academic programs at USIU-Africa: Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSc Nursing): integrating global health exposure, international perspectives, and clinically oriented training; Master of Science in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics: incorporating computational pharmacology, pharmacogenomics, precision medicine, and advanced clinical training; and Master of Science in Clinical Pharmacognosy and Complementary Medicine: integrating evidence-based complementary medicine, clinical assessment, and practical healthcare training.

The study highlights how interdisciplinary faculty expertise, institutional commitment to academic program expansion, hospital and industry partnerships, and USIU-Africa’s dual national and international accreditation environment supported curriculum innovation.

There are several key takeaways from the publication, highlighting important considerations for strengthening health professions education and ensuring that curriculum development remains relevant, sustainable, and responsive to evolving healthcare needs. The first is Curriculum innovation and competency-based education. Integrating emerging scientific disciplines, digital and precision-medicine approaches, global health perspectives and practical clinical training can strengthen competency-based health professions education and prepare graduates for evolving healthcare needs. Closely linked to curriculum innovation is the second takeaway: Stakeholder engagement and industry collaboration. Continuous engagement with clinicians, regulatory bodies, industry representatives, and employers was essential in aligning curricula with workforce expectations. These consultations also informed practical learning components, including clinical attachments and workplace-based training.

The third takeaway is Accreditation as a driver of quality improvement. National regulatory requirements and international accreditation standards provided complementary quality assurance. National processes supported contextual and professional compliance, while international accreditation encouraged learning-outcome alignment, institutional effectiveness, and continuous improvement. Beyond quality assurance, the publication also highlights the importance of ensuring that curriculum innovation is financially viable and institutionally supported. The fourth takeaway is Financial sustainability and institutional support. The study identifies program costing and resource requirements as important considerations, particularly for specialized postgraduate programs. It highlights the value of phased implementation, long-term strategic planning, and financial evaluation that considers both institutional sustainability and future workforce impact.

Finally, the fifth takeaway is Faculty recognition and sustainable curriculum innovation. Curriculum development requires substantial academic expertise, interdisciplinary teamwork, and sustained engagement. The publication stresses the importance of recognizing curriculum development as a scholarly contribution and of giving faculty the institutional support to keep innovating.

The publication emphasizes that curriculum innovation is not simply a technical exercise. It is a collaborative, iterative process that needs continuous negotiation among academic institutions, regulators, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders. It advocates early regulatory engagement, stronger partnerships between universities and industry, flexible approaches to emerging interdisciplinary programs, and sustainable institutional frameworks that support academic innovation.

Speaking to the CTW Team, Dr. Terefe expressed his sincere appreciation to USIU-Africa leadership, faculty colleagues, and the multidisciplinary curriculum development teams for their support, expertise, and contributions throughout the program development process.

“The publication highlights USIU-Africa’s contribution to advancing health sciences education. It adds to the ongoing conversation on strengthening Competency-Based Education and Training (CBET), promoting curriculum innovation, and preparing competent, practice-ready healthcare professionals in Kenya and beyond,” he noted.

To read the full article, visit: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44217-026-02287-y

Publication: Terefe EM. Reflective analysis of health sciences curriculum innovation at a Kenyan University. Discover Education. 2026;5:1213. DOI: 10.1007/s44217-026-02287-y. Open access.
